title: Maximum Average Pass Ratio
statement:
A school has several classes, each about to sit a final exam. `classes[i] = [pass_i, total_i]` says that class `i` has `total_i` students, of whom `pass_i` will pass. A class's pass ratio is its number of passing students divided by its number of students, and the average pass ratio is the mean of the pass ratios of all classes.

You also have `extraStudents` additional students who pass any exam they take. Place every one of them in some class (each extra student raises both the passing count and the size of the class it joins by 1), and return the largest average pass ratio you can achieve. Answers within `10^-5` of the exact value are accepted.
notes:
## Intuition

Adding one passing student to a class with ratio `pass / total` raises it by `(pass + 1) / (total + 1) - pass / total`, its **gain**. Every class counts equally in the average, so each extra student should go where the gain is largest right now. The gains of one class shrink as it receives more students (the ratio creeps towards 1 ever more slowly), so a greedy choice never blocks a better later one: putting each student where the current gain is largest gives the best total. A max-heap keyed by gain finds that class in O(log n) instead of scanning all classes for every student.

(The exact alternative is a knapsack-style DP over how many students each class gets, which costs O(n · extraStudents²).)

## Approach

1. Define `gain(pass, total)` as above, and make `heap` an array of `[gain, pass, total]` entries.
2. Turn `heap` into a max-heap on `gain` by calling `siftDown` on every parent, from the last one up to the root. `siftDown` swaps an entry with its larger child until neither child is larger.
3. For each extra `student`, take the root (the largest gain), replace it with the class after adding one passing student, `[gain(pass + 1, total + 1), pass + 1, total + 1]`, and sift it down.
4. Add up `pass / total` over the final entries into `sum` and return `sum / heap.length`.

## Example 1, step by step

The gains are `2/3 - 1/2 = 0.1667` for `[1,2]`, `4/6 - 3/5 = 0.0667` for `[3,5]` and `0` for `[2,2]`. The first student joins `[1,2]`, which becomes `[2,3]` with gain `3/4 - 2/3 = 0.0833`, still the largest, so the second student joins it too: `[3,4]`. The average is `(3/4 + 3/5 + 2/2) / 3 = 2.35 / 3 = 0.78333`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + extraStudents · log n): building the heap is O(n) and each student costs one sift-down.
- Space: O(n) for the heap.

## Pitfalls

- Ordering classes by their current ratio (helping the weakest class) is wrong: `[1,10]` gains less from a student than `[1,2]`.
- In Java or C, compute the gain with floating-point division; `(pass + 1) / (total + 1)` in integers is `0` for almost every class.
- A full class (`pass == total`) has gain `0` and should only receive students when every class is full.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gain(pass, total)` | how much one more passing student raises this class's ratio |
| `heap` | max-heap of `[gain, pass, total]` entries, largest gain at index 0 |
| `index`, `left`, `right`, `largest` | a heap position, its children, and whichever of the three has the largest gain |
| `student` | how many extra students have been placed |
| `sum` | total of the final pass ratios |
